items.title: What a parish is
items.summary: A parish is a stable community of the faithful in a diocese, entrusted to a pastor under the bishop. Only the bishop sets up, joins or closes parishes, after hearing the presbyteral council. A parish that is lawfully set up is a juridic person. Parishes are normally territorial; personal parishes (for a language or rite, for example) are also possible.

items.title: The pastor and his appointment
items.summary: The pastor is the proper shepherd of the parish, carrying out teaching, sanctifying and governing under the bishop, with the help of other priests, deacons and lay people. He must be a priest, is appointed by the diocesan bishop and should be someone suited to the parish's needs.

items.title: The pastor's duties
items.summary: The pastor sees that the word of God is preached, that the faithful are taught, that the Eucharist is the centre of parish life, that the sacraments are available (Confession included), and that he knows and visits his people, cares for the sick and dying and supports families. Some functions are entrusted especially to him, such as baptism, the sacrament of the sick, assisting at marriages and funerals.

items.title: The pastor represents the parish
items.summary: In all juridic matters the pastor acts on behalf of the parish, and he sees that its goods are administered according to canons 1281 to 1288. Contracts, property and bank matters run through him, within diocesan policy.

items.title: Residence, Mass for the people, parish registers
items.summary: The pastor lives in the parish, takes holidays within the limits set by law and offers Mass for the people of the parish on Sundays and holy days of obligation. Each parish keeps registers of baptisms, marriages and deaths (and others the bishop requires), with notes of confirmation and marriage added to the baptism entry. Registers and the parish seal are kept safely, and old registers are preserved.

items.title: The parish pastoral council
items.summary: If the bishop judges it opportune after hearing the presbyteral council, each parish has a pastoral council, presided over by the pastor, in which the faithful help promote pastoral activity. It has a consultative vote only and follows the norms the bishop sets.

items.title: The parish finance council
items.summary: Every parish must have a finance council, governed by universal law and the bishop's norms, in which members of the faithful help the pastor administer the parish's goods. Unlike the pastoral council, it is required in every parish.

items.title: Parochial vicars (associate pastors)
items.summary: Associate pastors help the pastor in the whole parish or in a defined part of it, are appointed by the bishop, live in or near the parish and share in the pastor's care under his authority. They offer Mass for the people when the pastor is unable and stand in for him as the law allows.

items.title: Catechumens are joined to the Church
items.summary: Catechumens, who ask by their own will to be incorporated into the Church, are already joined to her in a special way. The Church cares for them and grants them certain rights proper to Christians.

items.title: The catechumenate
items.summary: Those who express their wish to embrace faith in Christ are admitted to the catechumenate in liturgical rites after a time of precatechumenate, and are formed in Christian life through instruction and apprenticeship. Conferences of bishops issue statutes for the catechumenate.

items.title: The sacraments in general
items.summary: The sacraments are actions of Christ and the Church. Ministers may not refuse them to those who ask at the right time, are properly disposed and are not prohibited by law. Sacred ministers ask no fee beyond the offerings set by the competent authority, and take care that the poor are not deprived of the sacraments because of poverty.

items.title: Baptism: celebration and preparation
items.summary: Baptism is the gateway to the sacraments. Adults are prepared through the catechumenate; parents of an infant are instructed before the baptism. A name foreign to Christian sentiment is avoided. Baptism is normally celebrated in the parish church of the person to be baptized, and on a Sunday or at the Easter Vigil where possible.

items.title: Baptism: the minister
items.summary: The ordinary minister of baptism is a bishop, priest or deacon; the pastor has a special role. In case of necessity anyone with the right intention may baptize. The baptism of adults, at least those 14 and older, is referred to the bishop, who may celebrate it himself.

items.title: Baptism: who may be baptized; infants
items.summary: Every unbaptized person may be baptized. An adult must have shown the wish, be instructed and tested in the catechumenate and be urged to sorrow for sin; an adult baptized is confirmed and receives the Eucharist immediately after. Parents should have an infant baptized within the first weeks after birth. For an infant to be baptized licitly, at least one parent (or whoever lawfully takes their place) must consent, and there must be a founded hope that the child will be brought up Catholic; otherwise baptism is delayed and the reason explained.

items.title: Godparents (sponsors)
items.summary: One godparent, or one of each sex, is chosen. A godparent must be designated by the candidate or the parents, be at least 16 (unless the bishop sets another age or the pastor or minister grants an exception for a just cause), be a confirmed Catholic who has received the Eucharist and leads a life of faith, be free of any canonical penalty and not be the parent. A baptized non-Catholic may stand only as a Christian witness alongside a Catholic godparent.

items.title: Proof and recording of baptism
items.summary: If there is no godparent, there should be at least one witness to prove the baptism. The pastor of the place where the baptism was celebrated records it promptly in the baptismal register, with the names of the baptized, the minister, the parents and godparents and any witnesses, and the place and date of birth and baptism.

items.title: Confirmation: celebration and minister
items.summary: Confirmation binds the baptized more perfectly to the Church and strengthens them as witnesses. It is conferred by anointing with chrism on the forehead with the laying on of hands and the prescribed words. The ordinary minister is the bishop; a priest may confirm with the faculty from the law or the bishop (for example, when he baptizes or receives an adult into full communion).

items.title: Confirmation: candidates, sponsors, records
items.summary: Every baptized person not yet confirmed can be confirmed. Above the age of reason, the candidate must be suitably instructed, properly disposed and able to renew the baptismal promises. The sacrament is conferred at about the age of discretion unless the conference of bishops sets another age. A sponsor should be present, with the same qualifications as a godparent, and it is fitting that the baptismal godparent serve. Confirmations are recorded in the diocesan or parish confirmation register and noted in the baptismal register.

items.title: The Eucharist and its celebration
items.summary: The Eucharist is the summit and source of Christian worship and life. Only a validly ordained priest celebrates it in the person of Christ. The faithful take part actively. Priests are urged to celebrate daily; a priest may celebrate once a day, and the bishop may permit two (three on Sundays and holy days) for a just cause or pastoral need.

items.title: Receiving Holy Communion
items.summary: Any baptized person not prohibited by law may receive. Children receive first Communion once they have sufficient knowledge and careful preparation, after first Confession. Someone conscious of grave sin does not receive without first going to Confession, unless there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess. Communion may be received a second time the same day, within a Mass one takes part in. The faithful fast for one hour before Communion from food and drink except water and medicine; the elderly, the sick and those who care for them are exempt. Catholics receive at least once a year, in the Easter season unless a just cause moves it.

items.title: Reservation and adoration of the Eucharist
items.summary: The Eucharist is reserved in the parish church in a tabernacle that is immovable, solid and locked, in a prominent place suited to prayer, with a lamp burning before it. The church should be open to the faithful for some hours each day. Exposition of the Blessed Sacrament is encouraged, with adoration, according to the liturgical books.

items.title: Mass offerings (stipends)
items.summary: A priest may accept an offering to apply a Mass for a particular intention. Any appearance of trade is excluded. A separate Mass is applied for each offering accepted; priests are urged to celebrate for the poor without an offering. The amount is set by the provincial bishops (or by custom). Pastors keep a book recording each Mass intention, the offering and its celebration; the bishop reviews it each year. Combining several intentions in one Mass is allowed only within the limits of the law and diocesan policy.

items.title: The sacrament of Penance
items.summary: In Penance the faithful who confess their sins, are sorry and resolve to amend receive forgiveness from God through the priest's absolution. Individual and integral confession with absolution is the only ordinary way. General absolution is allowed only in the cases the law lists. The proper place is a church; a confessional with a fixed grille is available for those who wish it.

items.title: The confessor and the seal
items.summary: Only a priest with the faculty to hear confessions absolves validly; pastors and others in charge of souls must hear confessions when reasonably asked and should offer set times. The sacramental seal is inviolable: a confessor may never betray a penitent by word or in any manner, and interpreters and anyone who learns of a confession are bound to secrecy.

items.title: The penitent
items.summary: To receive the sacrament, the penitent turns away from sin with the resolve to amend. Grave sins are confessed in kind and number. After reaching the age of discretion, each of the faithful confesses grave sins at least once a year. Every member of the faithful is free to confess to any lawfully approved confessor, even of another rite.

items.title: Anointing of the Sick
items.summary: The Church commends the dangerously ill to the Lord through anointing with oil and prayer. It can be given to a member of the faithful who, having reached the use of reason, begins to be in danger because of sickness or old age; it can be repeated if the person recovers and falls ill again or the illness worsens. Every priest, and only a priest, administers it validly; pastors and those in charge of the sick are bound to provide it.

items.title: Marriage in general
items.summary: Marriage is a lifelong partnership of the whole of life between a man and a woman, ordered to their good and to the procreation and upbringing of children; between the baptized it is a sacrament. Its essential properties are unity and indissolubility. Consent, lawfully given, makes marriage, and no human power can supply it.

items.title: Marriage preparation and pre-nuptial checks
items.summary: Pastors provide preparation for marriage: preaching and catechesis, personal preparation of the couple, a fruitful liturgy and help for married couples afterwards. Before a marriage, it must be established that nothing stands in the way of a valid and licit celebration (the pre-nuptial investigation, following the conference of bishops' norms). Catholics not yet confirmed should be confirmed before marriage if possible. Certain cases, such as a marriage of those who have rejected the faith or a minor whose parents are unaware, need the bishop's permission.

items.title: Impediments to marriage
items.summary: A diriment impediment makes a person unable to marry validly. They include age (16 for a man and 14 for a woman in universal law; the conference of bishops may set a higher age for liceity), antecedent and perpetual impotence, an existing marriage bond, disparity of worship (a Catholic and an unbaptized person, dispensable), sacred orders, a public perpetual vow of chastity in a religious institute, abduction, crime and certain degrees of consanguinity, affinity, public propriety and adoption. Some can be dispensed by the bishop.

items.title: Matrimonial consent
items.summary: Consent must be given by persons capable of it, who know what marriage is and freely will it. Lack of sufficient use of reason, grave lack of discretion of judgement, psychological incapacity, certain errors, deceit, simulation, conditions about the future and force or grave fear can make consent invalid.

items.title: The form of marriage and its recording
items.summary: Catholics marry validly before the local ordinary, the pastor or a priest or deacon delegated by either, and two witnesses. Marriage is normally celebrated in the parish of one of the parties; elsewhere needs permission. After the celebration the pastor of the place records it in the marriage register, and it is noted in the baptismal registers of both spouses.

items.title: Mixed marriages
items.summary: A marriage between a Catholic and a baptized non-Catholic needs the permission of the competent authority. The Catholic party declares readiness to avoid dangers to the faith and promises sincerely to do all in their power to have the children baptized and raised Catholic; the other party is informed of these promises. Both are instructed on the purposes and essential properties of marriage. The bishop can dispense from the canonical form for grave difficulty.

items.title: Separation, dissolution and convalidation
items.summary: A ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or cause except death. The law also covers the Pauline privilege, dissolution of a non-consummated marriage, separation with the bond remaining, simple convalidation and radical sanation of an invalid marriage. Questions of nullity go to the diocesan tribunal, not the parish.

items.title: Church funerals
items.summary: Deceased members of the faithful are to be given a Church funeral according to the law. The Church earnestly recommends burial, but does not forbid cremation unless chosen for reasons contrary to Christian teaching. The funeral is normally celebrated in the deceased's own parish church, though another church may be chosen. Catechumens count as members of the faithful for funerals, and the bishop may permit a funeral for children whose parents intended to have them baptized but who died before baptism. A funeral is denied only in the cases the law names, unless there were signs of repentance before death; the parish refers doubtful cases to the bishop. Every funeral is recorded in the register of deaths.

items.title: Sundays and holy days of obligation
items.summary: Sunday is the primordial holy day. The universal law lists other holy days of obligation, but the conference of bishops may suppress some or move them to a Sunday. In Canada, besides every Sunday, the holy days of obligation are Christmas (25 December) and Mary, Mother of God (1 January). The obligation is fulfilled by taking part in Mass on the day or the evening before.

items.title: Days of penance
items.summary: All the faithful are bound to do penance. Every Friday and the season of Lent are penitential times. Abstinence from meat is kept on Fridays (or another penance the conference of bishops sets), and fasting and abstinence on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday. Abstinence binds from age 14; fasting binds from age 18 until the beginning of one's sixtieth year (the 59th birthday). Those who are ill or pregnant, among others, are excused.

items.title: Temporal goods: the right to own
items.summary: The Church has the innate right to acquire, keep, administer and dispose of goods for its own purposes: worship, support of clergy and ministers, the apostolate and charity, especially for the poor. A parish, as a juridic person, owns the goods it lawfully acquires, under the bishop's supervision.

items.title: Acquiring goods: support, collections, offerings
items.summary: The faithful are obliged to support the Church. The bishop can order special collections, and a parish takes up the collections he prescribes. Offerings given to the parish are presumed to be for the parish unless the donor said otherwise, and offerings given for a stated purpose may be used only for it. Begging for funds by private persons needs permission.

items.title: Administration of goods
items.summary: Administrators act in the name of the Church and with the care of a good householder. Every juridic person has a finance council or at least two advisers. Administrators take an oath, keep an inventory, insure property, observe civil law, collect income, pay employees a just wage, keep accounts in order and report annually to the bishop. Acts beyond ordinary administration need written permission according to diocesan norms. Accounts of offerings are given to the faithful according to norms set by particular law.

items.title: Contracts and alienation of property
items.summary: Civil contract law is observed as canon law unless it is contrary to divine law. Selling or otherwise alienating goods that form the stable patrimony of a parish above the limit set by the conference of bishops needs the permission of the competent authority (the bishop, with his finance council and college of consultors; above a higher limit, the Holy See). Leases and other transactions that could worsen the parish's financial position follow the same care.

items.title: Pious wills and foundations
items.summary: Bequests and gifts for pious causes are carried out with care, and the bishop oversees them. Pious foundations, such as a fund for Masses in perpetuity, are accepted only with the bishop's written permission, are recorded and their obligations are listed and kept in the parish. The bishop can reduce Mass obligations in certain cases when income has decreased.

items.title: The seven sacraments
items.summary: The Church celebrates seven sacraments instituted by Christ: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony. They touch every stage of Christian life and form an organic whole centred on the Eucharist.

items.title: Christian initiation and the catechumenate
items.summary: Becoming a Christian has, from the time of the Apostles, been a journey in stages: proclamation of the word, acceptance of the Gospel, conversion, profession of faith, Baptism, the gift of the Spirit and the Eucharist. The catechumenate for adults, restored by the Second Vatican Council, forms people through these stages.

items.title: The sacrament of Baptism
items.summary: Baptism frees from sin, gives new birth as children of God, makes us members of Christ and of the Church, and is the gateway to the other sacraments. It is celebrated with water and the Trinitarian formula, and leaves an indelible spiritual mark. The Church baptizes infants because of the free gift of grace, with parents and godparents responsible for their growth in faith.

items.title: The sacrament of Confirmation
items.summary: Confirmation completes baptismal grace, gives a special strength of the Holy Spirit, and binds the confirmed more perfectly to the Church as witnesses of Christ. It is given by anointing with chrism; in the Latin Church the bishop is the ordinary minister, showing the link with the apostolic Church.

items.title: The sacrament of the Eucharist
items.summary: The Eucharist is the source and summit of Christian life: the memorial of Christ's Passover, His sacrifice made present and His real presence under the appearances of bread and wine. It explains the structure of the Mass, Sunday as its heart, the conditions for receiving Communion, and adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.

items.title: The sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation
items.summary: Those who sin after baptism are reconciled with God and the Church through this sacrament. Its acts are contrition, confession and satisfaction by the penitent, and absolution by the priest. It explains the examination of conscience, the seal of confession and indulgences.

items.title: The Anointing of the Sick
items.summary: Through the anointing and prayer of the priest, the Church commends the sick to the suffering and glorified Lord. It gives strength, peace and courage, unites the sick person to Christ's Passion, and can forgive sins. It is fitting to receive it before surgery and when the elderly grow frail.

items.title: The sacrament of Holy Orders
items.summary: Through Holy Orders the mission Christ entrusted to the Apostles continues in the Church, in three degrees: bishops, priests and deacons. It explains the ministry of each degree and who may be ordained.

items.title: The sacrament of Matrimony
items.summary: Marriage is a covenant by which a man and a woman establish a lifelong partnership, raised by Christ to a sacrament between the baptized. It covers consent, the celebration of marriage, mixed marriages, the goods of marriage (unity, indissolubility, openness to children), and the family as the domestic church.

items.title: Sacramentals and popular piety
items.summary: Sacramentals are sacred signs, such as blessings, holy water and the Rosary, by which the Church prepares people to receive grace and sanctifies different circumstances of life. Popular devotions accompany the liturgy and should harmonize with it.

items.title: Christian funerals
items.summary: The Christian funeral commends the dead to God, supports the hope of the community, and expresses communion with the deceased. It normally includes the welcome of the community, the Liturgy of the Word, the Eucharist, and the farewell (final commendation).

items.title: The precepts of the Church
items.summary: The precepts set the minimum of prayer and moral effort: attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, confess serious sins at least once a year, receive Communion at least in the Easter season, keep the days of fasting and abstinence, and help provide for the needs of the Church.

items.title: The Lord's Day
items.summary: Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, is the first holy day of obligation. The faithful take part in the Eucharist and rest from work that hinders worship, joy, works of mercy and family life. Deliberately missing Sunday Mass without a serious reason, such as illness or caring for infants, is a grave matter.
